faqs.q: 1. How is packaging for a cafe burger different from a burger bar?
faqs.a: A cafe sleeve arrives into an existing set rather than starting one. There is already a cup, a lid, a bag and a napkin chosen for drinks, and the sleeve has to work with them. A burger bar picks packaging to suit burgers; a cafe picks packaging that also looks right beside a coffee.

faqs.q: 2. Can I match my sleeve colour exactly to my cups?
faqs.a: Rarely, and chasing it is usually wasted money. A cup is coated and often lined, a paper bag is absorbent, and a sleeve sits between them. The same ink lands differently on each. Matching tone, ink count, typeface and surface character reads as coherent even when the colour shifts.

faqs.q: 3. What quantity should a low-volume cafe order?
faqs.a: Work out honest weekly usage, multiply by the months you are willing to hold stock, and compare that against the minimum order before choosing artwork. Ordering eighteen months of stock ties up cash and space, and any branding change in that window turns the remainder into waste.

faqs.q: 4. Does packaging deteriorate if it sits in storage?
faqs.a: It can. Board held for a long period absorbs moisture, particularly in a cupboard near a dishwasher or under a counter, and loses stiffness. Marks accumulate on stock stored loose. What arrives after a year in a damp cupboard is not the board that was approved.

faqs.q: 5. Should I use different sleeves for dine-in and takeaway?
faqs.a: At cafe volumes, usually not. Running two lines for one item rarely pays. A single sleeve leaning slightly towards the takeaway requirement is the common compromise, because a closure failing in a bag is more visible to a customer than a slightly plain sleeve on a plate.

faqs.q: 6. Do breakfast items need a different sleeve?
faqs.a: Often. A folded egg on a soft roll behaves differently from a beef patty — it is usually shorter, softer and more prone to compression. Measure it separately rather than assuming the burger sleeve covers it, especially if the roll is a different diameter.

faqs.q: 7. Is white board a good choice for a cafe?
faqs.a: It suits warmly lit interiors and keeps food looking fresh on a plate. The trade-off is that light board shows grease and handling marks readily, which matters when the sleeve sits under a customer's eye through a meal. Resolve that against how sauced your hot menu actually is.

faqs.q: 8. How many sleeve sizes should a cafe stock?
faqs.a: As few as the menu tolerates. Counter space is short and already crowded, so each variant competes for reach. Group items by their limiting dimension rather than by menu category, which usually produces a smaller set than expected.

faqs.q: 9. What if the printed minimum order is too large?
faqs.a: A plain sleeve carrying a small applied mark keeps a branded look without committing to a large artwork run. It also means a menu or branding change does not strand a year of printed stock. Ask what the minimum actually is before assuming it rules printing out.

faqs.q: 10. Does a matte or gloss finish suit a cafe better?
faqs.a: Matte is generally easier to match across a mixed counter set, because it sits quietly beside cups and bags rather than reflecting differently from them. Gloss makes printed colour denser, which is more useful when the artwork is colour-led than when it is a simple mark.

faqs.q: 11. Will sleeves work for light meals other than burgers?
faqs.a: They are used for toasted sandwiches, breakfast rolls and similar handheld items. The question is whether the item holds a shape the sleeve can grip. Anything that flattens significantly, or is much longer than it is tall, may suit a different format.

faqs.q: 12. How do I keep the counter set looking consistent over time?
faqs.a: Retain approved physical samples of each item and check reorders against them, and reorder related items at similar times where possible. Drift usually appears when one part of the set is reprinted alone and then sits next to older stock.

faqs.q: 1. What makes street food packaging different from takeaway packaging?
faqs.a: It is used standing up with no surface to rest anything on. One hand is usually occupied, the customer may be walking, and the sleeve is the only barrier between the food and their clothing. Everything has to work one-handed from handover to disposal.

faqs.q: 2. Why does grip matter more at a street stall?
faqs.a: Because the sleeve is held continuously through the whole meal rather than set down between bites. It needs enough depth for fingers to close around, enough stiffness not to fold under a squeeze, and a shape that does not let the build slide out when tilted upward to eat.

faqs.q: 3. How is sauce different from grease as a packaging problem?
faqs.a: Sauce is more mobile. It travels sideways as well as down and reaches the sleeve mouth rather than only the base, often on the first bite. A barrier treatment aimed at rendered fat does not necessarily address a sauce escaping from the side of a build.

faqs.q: 4. Can a sleeve be made leakproof for wet builds?
faqs.a: No, and it should not be described that way. What helps is depth at the mouth, a wall high enough to contain a spill before it reaches the hand, and an inner greaseproof wrap. Together those buy the time a customer needs to finish rather than sealing anything.

faqs.q: 5. Does hot weather really change sleeve performance?
faqs.a: Noticeably. Fat is more liquid at higher temperatures and moves into fibre faster, so a build that marks a sleeve in fifteen minutes indoors can do it in five on a hot pavement. A sleeve judged on a mild test day will behave differently on a summer weekend.

faqs.q: 6. How should stock be stored at an outdoor stall?
faqs.a: Sealed and out of direct sun. Humid air softens board and leaves an open case limp by the end of a shift, and sun warms the sleeve before food is even loaded. Never keep an open tray of sleeves exposed on the counter.

faqs.q: 7. How do I stop sleeves blowing away at an open stall?
faqs.a: A closed dispenser or a weighted tray. Flat sleeves in an open tray go over the side in any breeze, and retrieving them mid-service is time you do not have. It costs almost nothing and removes a recurring irritation.

faqs.q: 8. What makes a handover work in a busy queue?
faqs.a: The burger must already be seated and the closure checked before you turn to the customer, because there is no chance to adjust afterwards. Offer the sleeve end-on so there is one obvious place to take it, and it can be gripped once and carried away in a single movement.

faqs.q: 9. How can customers tell similar orders apart in a queue?
faqs.a: A simple visual marker on the sleeve removes a conversation at the busiest moment. It can be printed, or it can come from the structure itself — a shaped opening or a distinguishing cut carried in the tooling rather than a separate print run.

faqs.q: 10. Will the sleeve fit the bags I already use?
faqs.a: Check rather than assume. Measure the bag and work backwards to a maximum sleeve size. A sleeve that has to be forced into a compact bag bends the closure, and a bent closure tends to work open later. Changing the bag is often cheaper than changing the sleeve.

faqs.q: 11. What board weight suits street service?
faqs.a: Usually stiffer than operators first expect, because a saturated sleeve fails while it is being held rather than while sitting on a plate. Give your supplier the build weight, how sauced it is and the fact that it will be eaten standing up, and ask what they would recommend.

faqs.q: 12. Should street food sleeves use an inner wrap?
faqs.a: For sauced or juicy builds, yes. The wrap does the barrier work while the sleeve provides grip and structure. On a menu eaten standing up, a wrap failure is on the customer's clothing rather than on a plate, which raises the cost of getting it wrong.

faqs.q: 13. How do I test a sleeve properly for street service?
faqs.a: Test at counter height with someone standing, not across a bench. Have them take it one-handed, eat from it while holding a drink, and walk while doing so. Watch where they grip and whether they re-grip after taking it — a re-grip means the shape needs work.

When a promotion runs across both takeaway and dine-in, the sleeve should feel uniform across settings. Keeping the same orientation rule and fold routine helps the message look consistent across photos, tables, and pickup shelves.

Five steps to keep bulk runs organized

  1. Keep promotional sleeves in a dedicated station position

  2. Use one orientation rule for every sleeve applied

  3. Separate burgers with a napkin layer in stacked bag orders

  4. Avoid overfilling bags so sleeves don’t press tightly together

  5. Do a quick corner check on the first tray of each rush wave

Five steps to protect sleeves on trays

  1. Place burgers away from tray edges to reduce rubbing

  2. Keep sauce cups in a separate tray zone, not against sleeves

  3. Avoid stacking burgers directly on top of each other on trays

  4. Use consistent spacing so sleeves do not scrape during carry

  5. Remove crushed sleeves from service to keep presentation uniform

Final Station Reset For Campaign Days

Campaign days run smoother when the station is reset between rush windows. Close open bundles to keep stacks flat, return cartons to their fixed positions, and remove sleeves that are bent at corners. Keep one sample sleeve nearby so staff can confirm orientation and fold behavior quickly. These small habits prevent repeated mistakes and keep messaging consistent through the full promotion window.

faqs.q: 1. How many promotional sleeves should I order?
faqs.a: Work from the campaign length rather than the price break. Estimate daily uptake from a comparable past promotion, multiply by campaign days, and add a modest margin for stronger performance. Surplus on a campaign line is waste rather than stock, so the cheapest unit price is often the most expensive total.

faqs.q: 2. Why does my QR code fail to scan from the sleeve?
faqs.a: Usually size, contrast or placement. A code needs enough physical area to resolve at arm's length, enough separation from the board colour for a camera to find the pattern, and a position away from folds and the grip zone. Test from a printed proof, not a screen.

faqs.q: 3. Can a QR code on a sleeve track campaign performance?
faqs.a: The printed code itself only carries a link. Whether scans can be counted, attributed or tied to redemptions depends entirely on what sits behind that link, which is a separate piece of work to set up. Do not assume the packaging provides measurement on its own.

faqs.q: 4. Where should the offer wording sit on the sleeve?
faqs.a: On the panel facing outward at handover, because that is the only moment the packaging has undivided attention. Terms and small print can go anywhere legible — they are read after the decision rather than before it.

faqs.q: 5. How do I decide artwork placement on a promotional sleeve?
faqs.a: Answer four physical questions first: which panel faces the customer at handover, which area disappears under a hand, which parts fold, and which surface the food is likely to mark. Those dictate placement more reliably than any layout preference.

faqs.q: 6. Is a screen proof enough for campaign artwork?
faqs.a: Not for anything with a code, a colour match or fine terms text. Those need to be seen printed, at size, on the intended board. A physical proof also shows how artwork sits once the sleeve is folded, which is never how it looks flat on screen.

faqs.q: 7. What should I check on a campaign proof?
faqs.a: Offer wording and dates against the signed brief, code scanning from the printed sheet with more than one phone, terms text read at arm's length, nothing important landing on a crease, and someone outside the project explaining what they think the offer means.

faqs.q: 8. Should campaign artwork replace my usual branding?
faqs.a: Better to sit on top of it. Sleeves that look unrelated to your normal packaging read as a different business during the period you most want recognition. Keep the logo, typeface and base colour, and let the campaign own a defined zone.

faqs.q: 9. What happens to leftover campaign stock?
faqs.a: It is generally unusable once the dates have passed, which is why quantity planning matters more here than on a standard line. Decide before ordering what you will do if uptake is lower than expected, rather than after the campaign ends.

faqs.q: 10. Can a promotional run be reordered mid-campaign?
faqs.a: That depends on lead time and press availability, and on a short campaign the reorder may arrive after the offer closes. Ask about realistic turnaround before setting the quantity, and treat a mid-campaign top-up as something to confirm rather than assume.

faqs.q: 11. Does full-coverage campaign artwork cause production issues?
faqs.a: It brings considerations rather than problems: heavy ink coverage over large solid areas shows mottling more readily, colour can drift across a long run, and folds through dense printed areas are more prone to visible cracking. All are reasons to review a full-size printed proof.

faqs.q: 12. How far ahead should a campaign sleeve be ordered?
faqs.a: Far enough that a proof can be reviewed properly and a correction made without threatening the launch date. Proofing is what gets compressed when other things slip, and it is the worst stage to shorten because a campaign sleeve cannot be quietly fixed on the next reorder.

faqs.q: 1. How do I work out how many sleeves an event needs?
faqs.a: Start from the format rather than the headcount. A seated dinner with one service is close to the guest number; buffet and station service runs above it; a late-night second serving runs well below. A public festival stand has no relationship to a headcount at all.

faqs.q: 2. How much overage should I order for an event?
faqs.a: Enough to cover stronger-than-expected uptake, decided deliberately before ordering. Unlike a restaurant there is no next week to absorb surplus, so the margin should reflect the risk of running short rather than a price break on a larger quantity.

faqs.q: 3. Whose logo should go on the customer-facing panel?
faqs.a: One mark, not two. That panel is the position with the most attention and splitting it between equal logos generally serves neither, because at handover a customer registers one thing at most. Secondary marks belong on a side or reverse panel.

faqs.q: 4. Can event-branded sleeves be reused at the next booking?
faqs.a: Not if they carry a date, a couple's names or a sponsor. That is why branded quantities should be ordered tight and plain quantities kept generous — plain stock behind a branded run turns a mid-service shortage into an inconvenience rather than a stoppage.

faqs.q: 5. How should stock be split between serving stations?
faqs.a: Not evenly. Stations near the entrance, the bar or the seating usually move more, and that is knowable from the floor plan in advance. Weight the initial split towards them and keep a central reserve rather than distributing every case at setup.

faqs.q: 6. What happens if one station runs out?
faqs.a: It stops serving regardless of what the others hold, which is why a central reserve and an agreed person to move stock matter. Counting remaining stock at a set point mid-service, rather than when it runs out, gives time to rebalance.

faqs.q: 7. Does storing packaging before an event cause problems?
faqs.a: It can. Board absorbs moisture from wherever it sits, and stock kept in a damp garage or a van for weeks does not fold like the approved sample. Keep cases sealed until setup and store them flat rather than on edge.

faqs.q: 8. Should I check stock before the event starts?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the highest-value habit on this list. Open one case and form a sleeve at setup. Finding a problem then leaves time to adapt; finding it at first service does not.

faqs.q: 9. How do mixed portions affect event planning?
faqs.a: They multiply the ways a station can run short, because each size has its own count. Events serving both full burgers and smaller items usually plan the two quantities separately rather than deriving one from the other.

faqs.q: 10. Is event packaging handled differently from restaurant stock?
faqs.a: It is handled far more. Cases are loaded, unloaded, moved to a station and often moved again, and each handling risks a crushed or opened case. A crushed case on the morning of an event is not recoverable, so packing and transport deserve attention.

faqs.q: 11. How far in advance should event sleeves be ordered?
faqs.a: Far enough that a proof can be checked and a correction made without risking the date, and with storage arranged for the interval. The interval itself is part of the plan, because where stock sits for those weeks affects what condition it arrives in.

faqs.q: 12. How can I improve quantity estimates for future events?
faqs.a: Record actual usage against the guest count and the format after each booking. Two or three recorded events give a far better basis than any general rule, because uptake depends heavily on the specific style of service and the crowd.

faqs.q: 13. What should be done with surplus on the night?
faqs.a: Reseal and store it properly before it goes into a van, not a week later. Most event packaging that gets written off is lost to handling after the event rather than to over-ordering.
